subtopic: Tragedy of the commons
passage: At the playschool's birthday circle, Miss set one big bowl of laddoos in the middle. "Share nicely." Suraj, five, saw Wasim grab two, so he grabbed three, fast, before they could go. Wasim grabbed four more. In a minute the bowl was empty. Little Pema, who was shy, got none and began to cry. Suraj looked at his sticky hands full of laddoos. He hadn't even wanted three. Miss knelt down. "What happened to the bowl?" Suraj mumbled, "Everybody took fast so nobody else could." Slowly, he put one laddoo in Pema's hand.

qa.q: How many laddoos did Suraj grab?
qa.a: Three.

qa.q: Why did Suraj grab three laddoos so fast?
qa.a: He saw Wasim grab two and worried the laddoos would be gone if he waited.

qa.q: What could Miss try next time with a shared bowl?
qa.a: She could pass the bowl around so each child takes one per turn, so nobody feels they must grab first.

qa.q: What was it like for Pema when the bowl emptied?
qa.a: Pema, who was shy, got none and cried, left out because everyone rushed.

grounding: Young children at a shared bowl each grab quickly for fear the others will take it all, and the shared treat is gone before everyone gets some.

subtopic: Tragedy of the commons
passage: I'm Jahnavi, and at my little brother Rafiq's fifth birthday I was in charge of the chocolate tin. I opened it in the middle of the rug and said, "Take some." For a second nobody moved. Then his friend Ivan grabbed a fistful, and every hand dived in at once. Rafiq pushed in too, stuffing chocolates into his pockets, his eyes on the others. The tin was empty in less than a minute. Two smaller kids got nothing. Rafiq had eleven chocolates and a smeared face, and he didn't look happy. He looked worried, as if someone might take them.

qa.q: How many chocolates did Rafiq end up with?
qa.a: Eleven chocolates.

qa.q: What does Rafiq's worried look suggest?
qa.a: He seemed afraid someone might take his chocolates, even though he had grabbed so many.

qa.q: What could Jahnavi try the next time Jahnavi is in charge of the tin?
qa.a: Jahnavi could hand out chocolates one round at a time, so no one has to rush to get a share.

qa.q: How might the two smaller kids feel when the tin is empty?
qa.a: They probably feel left out and sad, having got nothing because they were slower.

grounding: An older sibling watches young children grab from a shared tin once one starts, emptying it so the slower ones get nothing.

subtopic: Tragedy of the commons
passage: Monday. Nani set down a plate of mango slices for Nikita and her cousin Tanuja. Nikita grabbed five at once, before Tanuja could. Tanuja grabbed the rest. Nani came back to an empty plate and two sticky, cross girls. Wednesday. Same plate. Nikita's hand shot out, then stopped. But Tanuja was already reaching, so both grabbed, and a slice fell on the floor. Friday. Nani put the plate down and said, "One each, then wait." Nikita took one. Tanuja took one. Back and forth they went, counting. One slice was left. They looked at each other. "Halves?" said Tanuja.

qa.q: How many mango slices did Nikita grab on Monday?
qa.a: Five at once.

qa.q: Why did Nikita's hand stop and then grab anyway on Wednesday?
qa.a: She seemed to remember Monday, but when she saw Tanuja reaching she worried she'd miss out and grabbed anyway.

qa.q: What choice did Nani make on Friday, and why did it work?
qa.a: Nani set a rule of one each, then wait, so neither girl had to rush to get her share.

qa.q: What might Tanuja be feeling when she offers 'Halves?'
qa.a: Tanuja seems relaxed and fair now, trusting that sharing the last slice will not leave her short.

grounding: Two young cousins grab from a shared plate because each fears the other will take it, until a simple turn-taking rule lets them share.

subtopic: Tragedy of the commons
passage: Monday. After lunch, Vasudha, nine, left the school tap dribbling while she chatted with Parul. "One tap won't empty the tank," she said. Across the yard, other taps dribbled too. Wednesday. By the last period the tank was dry. Class 4 couldn't wash their tiffins, and the toilets smelled. The peon said every tap had been left open a little. Vasudha went quiet. She had thought it was only hers. Friday. Vasudha and Parul made signs in fat crayon: "Close me! Every drop is ours." They taped one above each tap. At break Vasudha caught herself about to walk away, and turned the tap off with a firm twist.

qa.q: What did Vasudha and Parul write on the signs?
qa.a: "Close me! Every drop is ours."

qa.q: Why did Vasudha go quiet on Wednesday?
qa.a: She realised her dribbling tap was one of many, and felt guilty for thinking only hers wouldn't matter.

qa.q: What choice did Vasudha and Parul make on Friday, and why could it help?
qa.a: They taped signs above each tap, reminding everyone that every drop is shared, so each person turns the tap off.

qa.q: What was Wednesday like for Class 4?
qa.a: They couldn't wash their tiffins and had to put up with smelly toilets, paying for everyone's dribbling taps.

grounding: A girl leaves a school tap running, sure one tap cannot matter, until everyone doing the same empties the shared tank.

subtopic: Tragedy of the commons
passage: Jeevan Dadu pointed his stick at the green pond. "Rashmi, when I was ten, you could see fish in that water. Every child in the village swam there after school. And every one of us threw our sugarcane peels and paper in it. I used to think, 'My peel is so small. What difference can it make?' Everybody thought the same. One summer the water turned green and smelly. The fish floated up, belly first. The panchayat closed the pond, and we had nowhere to swim. That summer was long and hot and sad. That's why I still pick up peels along the bank."

qa.q: What did the children throw into the pond?
qa.a: Sugarcane peels and paper.

qa.q: What did young Jeevan think about his own peel?
qa.a: He thought it was so small it couldn't make a difference.

qa.q: What choice does Jeevan make now because of that summer?
qa.a: He still picks up peels along the bank, having learned that everyone's small peels together ruined the pond.

qa.q: How might Rashmi see a single wrapper after hearing this story?
qa.a: Rashmi may see it as part of a pile made by everyone, not a harmless little thing.

grounding: A grandfather recalls how, as a boy, he and every other child littered a village pond thinking one peel didn't matter, until it was spoiled.

subtopic: Tragedy of the commons
passage: The colony had one good cricket bat, bought with everyone's pocket money, and dark clouds were rolling in. Jatin, eleven, got it first and wouldn't let go. "Just one more over. Then Ramesh." Ramesh waited. So did the others. When Jatin was finally out, Ramesh grabbed the bat and kept it just as long. Then the next kid did the same. Nobody passed it on. They yanked it back and forth, arguing, and it slipped onto the wet concrete in the first drops of rain. The handle cracked. They stood in the drizzle, staring at it. "I only kept it a bit," Jatin muttered. "So did we all," said Ramesh.

qa.q: How was the colony's cricket bat bought?
qa.a: With everyone's pocket money.

qa.q: What was Jatin thinking in muttering 'I only kept it a bit'?
qa.a: Jatin felt that one person's extra time was too small to be the cause, not seeing that everyone had thought the same.

qa.q: What could the children agree on to protect the next bat?
qa.a: A fixed number of overs each, with the bat passed on in turn, so no one needs to hog it.

qa.q: What does Ramesh's reply 'So did we all' show about how Ramesh sees what happened?
qa.a: Ramesh sees that each of them took a little extra, and together that spoiled the bat they all owned.

grounding: Children each hog a shared cricket bat a little, thinking one person's share doesn't matter, until the fighting over it breaks the bat.

subtopic: Tragedy of the commons
passage: Teacher's note, Class 11 project week. Written by Lokesh Sir. Shankar stayed back today and told me what he had noticed in his group of five. Meenal and Zubin had done almost all the research and the slides, while the other three, Shankar included until last week, kept saying, "We'll do it tomorrow." He said, "Sir, nobody's name is on any part, so nobody's responsible. The two careful ones end up doing everything, and today Meenal snapped at all of us." He said he felt bad about his own part. I have changed the project sheet: each member now signs for a named section, and there is a short check-in every Thursday. Shankar asked to take the data section.

qa.q: How many students were in Shankar's group?
qa.a: Five.

qa.q: Why did Shankar feel bad when he spoke to Lokesh Sir?
qa.a: He had been one of the three putting work off until last week, so he felt partly responsible for Meenal and Zubin carrying the load.

qa.q: What did Lokesh Sir change, and why should it help?
qa.a: Each member now signs for a named section with a Thursday check-in, so everyone is accountable and the careful two no longer carry everything.

qa.q: What might Meenal's snapping reveal about how Meenal felt?
qa.a: Meenal likely felt resentful and worn out after doing most of the research and slides while others kept postponing.

grounding: A student recognises that with no one accountable in a group project, two careful members carry the work and grow resentful, and the teacher adds named roles.

subtopic: Tragedy of the commons
passage: Thursday. I'm one of the four boys in our geography project group, and today I finally saw what's been going on. Chinmay and Esther have done everything: the map, the report, the model of the river. The rest of us "helped" by sending thumbs-up in the group chat. Today Esther stayed back till six gluing labels while Abel and Sunny went to play football. Nobody is in charge of anything, so nobody feels guilty. Chinmay didn't complain, but when Sunny said, "Great work, team!" he went very quiet and packed up without saying bye. I think he's fed up. Honestly, I would be. Tomorrow I'm taking the labels home and doing the river section myself. And I'm going to suggest we each put our name on one part. - Thomas

qa.q: Until what time did Esther stay back?
qa.a: Till six.

qa.q: What does Chinmay packing up without saying bye suggest he felt?
qa.a: He seemed fed up and resentful that Esther and he did everything while the others shared the credit.

qa.q: What two choices does Thomas make for tomorrow, and why do they matter?
qa.a: Taking the labels home and doing the river section, and suggesting each person names one part, so the load is shared and everyone is accountable.

qa.q: How might Esther feel hearing 'Great work, team!'?
qa.a: Esther may feel irritated, since the team credit covered work that Esther and Chinmay mostly did.

grounding: A boy notices that in his group, with nobody accountable, two careful members carry the project and start to resent it, and he decides to change his part.

subtopic: Tragedy of the commons
passage: By Friday the pantry on the third floor of the women's hostel had a sink full of sticky pans and a smell nobody wanted to name. Uma, twenty, stood in the doorway with her one mug. She had left a plate there on Monday, meaning to wash it later. So, it seemed, had everyone. Jaya came in behind her. "Whose is all this?" "Everyone's," said Uma. "And no one's." Jaya laughed without much humour. "I left a bowl. I thought one bowl didn't matter." "I thought one plate didn't matter." They looked at the tower of dishes, every piece of it somebody's "just one." Uma rolled up her sleeves. "Let's at least do ours." Jaya picked up a sponge, then hesitated. "And the rest?"

qa.q: On which floor was the pantry?
qa.a: The third floor of the women's hostel.

qa.q: What did Uma think when she left her plate on Monday?
qa.a: She meant to wash it later and assumed one plate didn't matter.

qa.q: What choice do Uma and Jaya face at the end, and what might help beyond that night?
qa.a: Whether to wash only their own dishes or the rest too; a shared rota for the pantry could stop the pile from coming back.

qa.q: How might other hostel residents feel walking into the pantry on Friday?
qa.a: They may feel disgusted and annoyed, while quietly knowing that one of the dishes is theirs.

grounding: Hostel residents each leave one dish in a shared pantry, sure their bit is too small to matter, until the mess spoils it for everyone.

subtopic: Tragedy of the commons
passage:
Subject: Our flat's kitchen, a confession

Hi Rajni,

You asked how flat life in Pune is going. The honest answer: our kitchen is a disaster, and I'm part of why. There are four of us. Each of us leaves just a cup or a pan, sure somebody else will deal with it, or that one pan is too small to count. Last week I found an ant trail from the sink to the sugar tin, and I wanted to blame the others. Then I counted: two of the dirty pans were mine. Nobody cooks there now because it's too gross, so we all spend money on takeaway. Funny, isn't it? Each of us saved five minutes, and together we lost the whole kitchen. I'm proposing a washing rota at our flat meeting on Sunday. Wish me luck.

Love,
Jasleen

qa.q: How many of the dirty pans were Jasleen's?
qa.a: Two of the dirty pans.

qa.q: What did Jasleen want to do on finding the ant trail, and what changed that?
qa.a: Jasleen wanted to blame the others, but counting the pans showed two were Jasleen's own.

qa.q: What is Jasleen proposing on Sunday, and why could it work?
qa.a: A washing rota, which makes each person's share visible so no one can assume someone else will clean.

qa.q: How might the other flatmates react to the proposal?
qa.a: They may feel defensive at first, but since nobody can cook in the kitchen now, they may welcome a fair rota.

grounding: A student admits that each flatmate, including themselves, leaves small messes assuming someone else will clean, until the shared kitchen is unusable.

subtopic: Tragedy of the commons
passage: "Jahnavi, you'll laugh, but I learned economics from a frying pan." Akash grinned, though he sounded a little embarrassed. "Five of us in the PG shared one kitchen. First week, spotless. subtopic: Tragedy of the commons
subtype: Setting rules everyone can live with [Response]
passage: In the village at the foot of the hills, the one tank that fed everyone's fields sank lower every summer. Farmers pumped whenever they liked, each sure their own share was too small to matter. Maria, twenty-five, back home after an agriculture diploma, stood up at the gram sabha. She did not scold. She pinned up a chart: a pumping day for each field, a painted mark on the tank wall as the limit, and two households each week to check the level. Anyone pumping out of turn would lose their next day. Simran's father scoffed. "Who will follow it?" "I will, first," Maria said, and that week she pumped her family's field only on its day, while the whole lane watched. By the end of the month the mark was holding, and Simran's father was one of the two checkers.

qa.q: What marked the limit on the tank?
qa.a: A painted mark on the tank wall.

qa.q: What did Maria want the village to see when she pumped only on her family's day?
qa.a: She wanted them to see she would follow the rule herself first, so they could trust it.

qa.q: Which part of Maria's plan made it hard to cheat, and why?
qa.a: Two households checking the level each week, with a lost pumping day for anyone out of turn, which made watching shared and consequences agreed.

qa.q: How did Simran's father's view change, and what might explain it?
qa.a: He scoffed at first but became a checker, likely because he saw Maria keep the rule and the mark hold.

grounding: A young woman proposes a fair pumping rota, a visible limit and shared checking for a village tank, keeps the rule first herself, and wins the village's trust.

subtopic: Tragedy of the commons

passage: The community garden behind the flats in Accra had one hose and a lot of thirsty tomatoes. People watered whenever they felt like it, some for an hour, and by March the tank was often empty by noon. Kofi, twenty-four, who grew okra in plot 6, wrote a proposal on a whiteboard at the gate: morning slots by plot number, fifteen minutes each, a shared logbook on a nail, and anyone who ran over twice would skip a day. Dalia, from plot 2, frowned. "You'll be the first to break it." "Then write my name in the book," Kofi said. For a week he watered at six, fifteen minutes on the dot, and signed each time. Neighbours started checking the book, and then signing it too. The tank lasted until evening.

qa.q: How long was each watering slot?
qa.a: Fifteen minutes each.

qa.q: What does Dalia's frown and remark suggest Dalia thought?
qa.a: Dalia doubted Kofi, suspecting the person proposing rules would not keep them.

qa.q: How did Kofi answer that doubt, and why did it work?
qa.a: He asked for his name to go in the book and then watered on the dot and signed every time, so neighbours saw the rule was fair and kept.

qa.q: How might the tomato growers feel when the tank lasts until evening?
qa.a: They are likely relieved and more trusting, since their plants now get water and the logbook shows everyone sharing fairly.

grounding: A young gardener proposes watering slots, a limit, a shared logbook and an agreed penalty for a common tank, and models the rule first.

passage: When the power went, Vasudha and Parul carried their trading game to the balcony and played by candlelight. The rule was simple: each puts a card face down. If both play "trade", each wins five coins. If one plays "steal" while the other trades, the stealer gets ten and the trader nothing. Three rounds, both traded. Then Vasudha's heart thumped. Parul hated losing. What if she steals now? I'll look so silly. Vasudha slid a "steal" card down. Parul flipped hers: "trade." Parul stared at the ten coins going across. "Why?" Vasudha's face burned in the candlelight. "I thought you would first."

qa.a: Ten, and the trader nothing.

qa.q: What could Vasudha do next to rebuild the game with Parul?
qa.a: Vasudha could admit the fear, give back the extra coins and trade next round, so they can go back to both winning five.

qa.q: How might Parul feel after playing 'trade' and seeing the ten coins go to Vasudha?
qa.a: Parul likely feels hurt and surprised after trusting Vasudha, and may be tempted to steal next time.

grounding: A child in a trading game cheats for fear that a friend will cheat first and leave them looking foolish, spoiling a fair game.

subtopic: Prisoner's dilemma and cooperation vs defection

passage: In the stairwell of their Kochi apartment block, Jomon and Avni sat with their sticker albums, making a deal: Jomon's shiny whale for Avni's two jungle cats. He'd be the fool who gave his best one for nothing. On "two," he pulled the whale back into his lap. Avni had already stretched out her hand with the cats. She saw the whale go back, and her face fell. "You didn't trust me?" Jomon looked at the floor. He had kept his whale, but somehow it felt like losing.

grounding: A boy about to swap stickers pulls back because he fears being cheated first, and the fear of being the fool breaks a fair trade.

subtopic: Prisoner's dilemma and cooperation vs defection
passage: The biology presentation was due Monday, in the same week as three unit tests. Shreya and Nazia had split it: Shreya the slides, Nazia the research. On Thursday Shreya thought, Nazia's so careful, she'll probably cover the slides too. I'll study for chemistry. On Friday, with the power cutting out every evening, Nazia thought, Shreya always makes nice slides at the last minute. I'll do maths. On Sunday night each opened the shared file. It had a title and nothing else. By midnight they had pulled together a messy seven slides. On Monday the teacher gave them a C and wrote, "You two can do far better than this." Both had done well in their tests. Neither felt good.

qa.q: How many slides did they pull together by midnight?
qa.a: A messy seven slides.

qa.q: What did Shreya expect Nazia to do on Thursday?
qa.a: Shreya expected careful Nazia to cover the slides too, so Shreya could study chemistry.

qa.q: What could they have done on Thursday to avoid Sunday night?
qa.a: A quick check-in on the shared file, so each would see the other's plan and neither could assume the other would cover.

qa.q: How might the teacher see their C?
qa.a: The teacher saw two capable students producing weak work, and wrote that they can do far better, sensing effort was missing.

grounding: Two teenagers each skip their part of a joint presentation expecting the other to cover, so both end up worse off than if they had cooperated.

subtopic: Prisoner's dilemma and cooperation vs defection
passage: At the tuition centre in Chembur, Francis and Ankita were paired for a ten-minute history talk on the salt march. They agreed to rehearse on Tuesday and Thursday. On Tuesday Ankita messaged, "Can't come, cousin's engagement. You're so good at speaking, you'll manage." Francis felt a small relief. If Ankita wasn't bothering, why should he? On Thursday he skipped too, telling himself Ankita would read up at home. On Saturday they stood before the class with one printed page each. Francis forgot the dates. Ankita lost her place twice. The talk lasted four minutes. Afterwards, on the stairs, Ankita said, "I thought you'd carry it." Francis said, "I thought you would." They both laughed, but not happily.

qa.q: How long did their talk last?
qa.a: Four minutes.

qa.q: Why did Francis feel a small relief at Ankita's message?
qa.a: He took it as permission to skip too, thinking that if Ankita wasn't bothering, he needn't either.

qa.q: Where did things go wrong, and what could Francis have done at that point?
qa.a: At Thursday's rehearsal; Francis could have messaged Ankita to fix a new time instead of assuming she would read up at home.

qa.q: What is it like for Ankita on the stairs when Francis says 'I thought you would'?
qa.a: Ankita realises they both counted on the other, and feels embarrassed and let down by both of them.

grounding: Two teenagers preparing a talk each skip rehearsal expecting the other to carry it, and the joint result is worse for both.

subtopic: Prisoner's dilemma and cooperation vs defection
passage: "Did you do the survey part?" Rehana asked in the school library, dropping her bag. "Me? I thought you were doing it." Zainab looked up from her notes. "We said we'd both do it." "Yes, but you always overdo things. I figured you'd finish it anyway." "And I figured you'd feel guilty and finish it." They stared at each other. "So nobody asked the thirty students." "Nobody asked anybody." "It's due at two." Zainab checked the clock. "It's twelve-forty." "If we'd each done fifteen, it'd be done." "And instead we each did zero." Rehana sat down hard. "Okay. You take the canteen, I'll take the field. Fifteen each. Go." They ran.

qa.q: How many students were they supposed to survey?
qa.a: Thirty students.

qa.q: What did Rehana expect Zainab to do, and why?
qa.a: Rehana expected Zainab to finish the survey anyway, because Zainab always overdoes things.

qa.q: What choice did they make at twelve-forty, and why was it better?
qa.a: They split the survey fifteen each, canteen and field, so each did a clear part instead of waiting for the other.

qa.q: How does Zainab's reason for skipping mirror Rehana's?
qa.a: Zainab figured Rehana would feel guilty and finish it, the same bet Rehana made, so both lost.

grounding: Two teenagers each leave a joint survey to the other, so neither does it, and they end up rushing when a fair split would have left both better off.

subtopic: Prisoner's dilemma and cooperation vs defection
passage: All semester Tejas had shared his neat economics notes with Hrithik, the boy in the next hostel room, who photographed every page. Hrithik always said, "I'll send you mine for the next unit," and never did. When results went up on the college board, Hrithik was third. Tejas was ninth. In the canteen, Tejas heard Hrithik tell someone, "My own notes were rubbish, honestly." Tejas's face went hot. He felt like the biggest fool on campus. That night, when a first-year, Mahesh, knocked and asked shyly to borrow his notes for the next test, Tejas said, "No. I don't share any more," and shut the door. Lying awake, he wondered whether Mahesh would have been different.

qa.q: What rank did Hrithik get?
qa.a: Third.

qa.q: What did Tejas feel when he heard Hrithik in the canteen?
qa.a: His face went hot; he felt like the biggest fool on campus, angry that his generosity had been used.

qa.q: What could Tejas try instead of refusing everyone?
qa.a: He could share with people who share back, starting small with Mahesh and seeing whether it is returned, rather than shutting everyone out.

qa.q: What was it like for Mahesh when Tejas shut the door?
qa.a: Mahesh, who asked shyly, was refused for something Mahesh had nothing to do with, and may feel confused and hurt.

grounding: A student whose shared notes helped a non-sharing peer rank higher feels foolish and angry and refuses a newcomer, at the cost of a possible future partner.

subtopic: Prisoner's dilemma and cooperation vs defection
passage: "Alka, can we split the law revision? I'll do contracts, you do torts, then we swap." Jasleen stood in the doorway of Alka's hostel room. "No." "No? You used to share with everyone." "Exactly. I shared with Farah all last year. She never gave me a single page, and she topped the class with my notes." Alka's voice shook. "I felt so stupid." "That's awful." "So I'm done. Everyone keeps their own notes." Jasleen sat on the bed. "Did I ever not give back?" "...No." "Then don't make me pay for Farah." Alka was quiet. "What if you do the same?" "Then stop sharing with me. Swap one chapter first. See what happens." Alka pulled out her torts file, slowly. "One chapter."

qa.q: Which subject did Jasleen offer to do?
qa.a: Contracts.

qa.q: How did Alka feel about sharing with Farah all last year?
qa.a: Alka felt stupid and hurt, because Farah never gave back and topped the class with Alka's notes.

qa.q: What small step does Jasleen propose, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Swapping one chapter first to see if it is returned, so Alka can test trust without risking everything.

qa.q: How does Jasleen see Alka's new rule of 'everyone keeps their own notes'?
qa.a: Jasleen sees it as unfair to people who always gave back, since it punishes them for what Farah did.

grounding: A student burned by a peer who used the student's notes and never shared back swears off sharing, until a friend points out that blanket distrust costs good partners.

subtopic: Prisoner's dilemma and cooperation vs defection
passage: I'm Deepak. In second year I helped Mahima with every circuits assignment. I'd stay up explaining, share my lab readings, even my old tests. She'd promise, "Next time I'll help you with maths." She never did. Then in the final practical she used my method word for word and got the top grade, while mine was marked "similar to another student." I was furious. More than that, I felt like an idiot. For the next year I shared nothing with anyone. I sat alone in the library. When project partners were assigned, I refused to swap notes, and our group scored lower than it should have. It took a patient lab partner, Joseph, returning every favour for months before I started to trust again. I still share. Just not blindly.

qa.q: What did Mahima promise to help Deepak with?
qa.a: Maths.

qa.q: What did Deepak feel after the final practical?
qa.a: Deepak was furious and, even more, felt like an idiot for having trusted Mahima.

qa.q: What was the turning point that let Deepak trust again?
qa.a: Joseph, a patient lab partner, returning every favour for months, which showed that not everyone takes without giving.

qa.q: How might Deepak's project group have been affected by the year of sharing nothing?
qa.a: The group scored lower than it should have, paying for a betrayal that wasn't theirs.

grounding: A student whose help was taken and used against them feels foolish and angry, swears off sharing, and learns that blanket distrust cost good partners.

subtopic: Prisoner's dilemma and cooperation vs defection
subtype: Cooperation that grows over repeated rounds [Actor]
passage: Week one. Disha and Mehak, both twenty and new at the bakery, agreed to cover each other's shifts when needed. Mehak covered Disha's Sunday. Disha covered Mehak's exam Friday. Easy. Month four. Disha got a chance to go to a concert and cancelled a promised cover for Mehak at the last minute. Mehak had to miss her cousin's wedding. For weeks after, Mehak double-checked every swap and asked for it in writing. Disha noticed, and felt the chill. Year two. Disha had never cancelled again. She had covered two of Mehak's Sundays without being asked. Slowly Mehak stopped asking for it in writing. "We'll be working together for ages," Disha said, sliding a tray into the oven. "I'd rather be someone you can count on."

qa.q: What did Mehak have to miss when Disha cancelled?
qa.a: Her cousin's wedding.

qa.q: What did Disha feel when Mehak started asking for swaps in writing?
qa.a: Disha felt the chill of lost trust, knowing the cancelled cover was remembered.

qa.q: What did Disha do to rebuild trust, and why did it work over time?
qa.a: She never cancelled again and covered two Sundays unasked, so steady reliability slowly outweighed the one betrayal.

qa.q: How did Mehak's view of Disha change between month four and year two?
qa.a: Mehak went from double-checking every swap to dropping the written requests, as Disha proved reliable again.

grounding: Two young coworkers learn over repeated shift swaps that one betrayal is remembered and steady reliability pays, since they will keep working together.

subtopic: Prisoner's dilemma and cooperation vs defection
subtype: Cooperation that grows over repeated rounds [Actor]
passage: Leela Nani wiped her glasses. "Seema, when I was nineteen I sold vegetables at the Thursday market, next to a girl called Meher who sold fruit. We made a pact: if one had to leave, the other would watch both stalls. For two years it worked. Then one Thursday, while Meher was away, her customers came to me, and I told them her mangoes were sour so they'd buy my cucumbers. Somebody told her. She didn't shout. She just stopped watching my stall. For months I lost sales whenever I had to leave early. We would be side by side every Thursday for years, and I had broken that for a few rupees. I apologised properly, with a basket of my best tomatoes. It took a whole season before she trusted me again. Keep your word with people you'll see again, beta."

qa.q: What did Leela tell Meher's customers?
qa.a: That Meher's mangoes were sour, so they'd buy Leela's cucumbers.

qa.q: What did Leela come to realise when Meher stopped watching her stall?
qa.a: She realised she had broken a long partnership with someone she would see every Thursday, for a few rupees.

qa.q: What did Leela do to repair it, and how long did it take?
qa.a: She apologised properly with a basket of her best tomatoes, and it took a whole season to regain Meher's trust.

qa.q: What was it like for Meher to learn what Leela had said?
qa.a: Meher felt betrayed by a trusted neighbour, and quietly withdrew her help rather than shouting.

grounding: A grandmother recalls how, as a young market vendor, one betrayal of a long stall partnership was remembered and cost her until she earned back trust.

subtopic: Prisoner's dilemma and cooperation vs defection
subtype: Cooperation that grows over repeated rounds [Actor]
passage: The power went out at the garage just as a truck driver pulled in needing his brakes fixed before a night run. Asif and Karthik, both twenty-one and three years into the job, had a system: whoever started a job, the other helped finish it, and any bonus was split. Tonight the owner offered the bonus to whoever finished first. Karthik could have jacked up the truck alone by torchlight and claimed the lot. He thought of Babu, a new mechanic who had grabbed a bonus from under Asif's nose last year; nobody would work with Babu after that, and he left within a month. Karthik held the torch while Asif bled the brakes. They finished at nine, in the dark, and split the money. "Same again tomorrow," Asif said. "Same again," said Karthik.

qa.q: What happened to Babu after he grabbed a bonus from under Asif's nose?
qa.a: Nobody would work with Babu, and he left within a month.

qa.q: What was Karthik thinking when he chose to hold the torch rather than finish alone?
qa.a: He remembered how Babu's grab cost him everyone's trust, and knew he would be working with Asif for years.

qa.q: Why does their system of splitting make sense for people who work side by side every day?
qa.a: Because they meet again tomorrow, reliably sharing work and money pays more over time than one grabbed bonus.

qa.q: How might Asif have felt if Karthik had claimed the whole bonus?
qa.a: Asif would likely feel betrayed after three years of splitting fairly and, as with Babu, might stop working with Karthik.

grounding: Two young mechanics who will keep working together choose cooperation over a one-time grab, knowing a betrayal would be remembered.

subtopic: Prisoner's dilemma and cooperation vs defection
passage: "Aparna, got a minute?" Rukmini pulled a chair up to Aparna's desk. "Sure. What's up?" "The client deck on Tuesday. The pricing model on slide four was mine. You presented it as your team's." Aparna's smile faded. "I... didn't think it mattered whose." "It matters to me. I shared it because we're on the same side, and I still want to be. But I need the credit when it's mine." A long pause. "You're right. I'll email the client team today and correct it." "Thank you." The next week Aparna's team was stuck on a forecasting sheet. Rukmini stopped by. "Want me to look at it with you?" Aparna blinked. "After last week?" "You fixed it. We're square."

qa.q: Which slide had Rukmini's pricing model?
qa.a: Slide four.

qa.q: What does Aparna's 'After last week?' suggest Aparna was feeling?
qa.a: Aparna was surprised and perhaps still embarrassed, not expecting Rukmini to help again so soon.

qa.q: What choices did Rukmini make, first about the deck and then the next week?
qa.a: Rukmini named the lost credit plainly and asked for it, then offered help once Aparna corrected it, avoiding both silence and a grudge.

qa.q: What would change if Rukmini had simply stopped sharing with Aparna?
qa.a: Aparna's team would lose a helpful colleague, and the two teams might drift into mutual distrust instead of working together.

grounding: A young professional who shared work openly calls out a colleague's taking of credit plainly, and cooperates again once the colleague corrects it.

subtopic: Prisoner's dilemma and cooperation vs defection
passage: I'm Irfan, and I freelance as a designer. When Pooja from the print shop down the lane first sent me work, I didn't haggle; I did it on time and did it well. She paid on time too. We traded favours for a year: I fixed her menus for free, she printed my cards at cost. Then she took on a rush job and handed my design to someone else to tweak, without asking, and billed it as her own. I didn't go silent or trash her online. I walked in and said, "That was my design. I'd have helped if you'd asked. You can't do that again." She looked embarrassed, apologised, and paid me for it that week. I went back to trading favours. Last month she sent me three new clients.

qa.q: What did Irfan fix for Pooja for free?
qa.a: Her menus.

qa.q: What did Irfan want Pooja to understand by walking in to speak?
qa.a: That the design was Irfan's, that help was there if asked, and that doing it again would not be okay.

qa.q: Which of Irfan's choices kept the relationship going after the breach?
qa.a: Naming the problem plainly in person instead of going silent or complaining online, then returning to trading favours once Pooja apologised and paid.

qa.q: How might Pooja see Irfan after that conversation?
qa.a: Pooja may respect Irfan as fair but firm, which may be why she later sent three new clients.

grounding: A young freelancer cooperates first, calls out a partner's misuse of their work plainly, and forgives once she makes it right, keeping a good partnership.

subtopic: Prisoner's dilemma and cooperation vs defection
passage: Supervisor's note, 30 September. Written by Chaitanya. Pradeep, twenty-four, has handled his first year with the warehouse team well. From day one he shared his order forecasts early and helped them plan, though that isn't strictly his job. They returned it: faster dispatches, early warnings about stock. In August their lead, Mr Bose, quietly blamed Pradeep's forecast for a late shipment that was really a warehouse error. Pradeep didn't sulk or start holding his forecasts back. He sent a short, plain email with dates showing where the delay happened and asked for the record to be corrected. Mr Bose called him, admitted it, and fixed the record. Pradeep went straight back to sharing forecasts. The two teams now work together better than any pair on this floor.

qa.q: Who quietly blamed Pradeep's forecast for the late shipment?
qa.a: Mr Bose, the warehouse team's lead.

qa.q: What did Pradeep likely feel when he was blamed, and what shows he kept a cool head?
qa.a: He was probably hurt and annoyed at being wrongly blamed, but he sent a short, plain email with dates rather than sulking.

qa.q: What did Pradeep do after Mr Bose admitted the error, and why was that wise?
qa.a: He went straight back to sharing forecasts, forgiving the slip so the teams didn't fall into mutual punishment.

qa.q: How might Mr Bose see Pradeep after the email?
qa.a: Mr Bose likely respects Pradeep more for being direct but fair, and trusts that Pradeep won't hold a grudge.

grounding: A young professional cooperates first with another team, calls out an unfair blame plainly with evidence, and resumes cooperation once it is corrected.
